   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in maritime transport, known as FuelEU Maritime, and applies in the European Union. «This Regulation lays down uniform rules imposing: (a) a limit on the greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity of energy used on board by a ship arriving at, staying within or departing from ports under the jurisdiction of a Member State; and (b) an obligation to use on-shore power supply (OPS) or zero-emission technology in ports under the jurisdiction of a Member State.» The Regulation was adopted as stated: «Done at Strasbourg, 13 September 2023.» The Official Journal reference is «OJ L 234, 22.9.2023».

**Document date:** 30 October 2026

Next scheduled review: *Analytical inference:* the Commission evaluation report due by 31 December 2027 (quoted in section 6) is the next scheduled review of the Regulation.

Statements of what the text requires are marked *Legal Confirmation Required:* where the role of a freight forwarder is not named in the text. *Industry interpretation:* marks material from a classification society and is not legal authority. *Analytical inference:* marks a reading that goes beyond the words quoted, with the fact it rests on named. The Commission's own question-and-answer document is cited as guidance from the Commission's services; it states that it does not commit the Commission. Sections 9 and 13 are left out because no product-specific content and no adjacent research is sourced for this Regulation.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

FuelEU Maritime sets a yearly limit on the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board ships, and requires containerships and passenger ships to use on-shore power supply or a zero-emission technology at the quayside. The objective is stated as: «Its objective in doing so is to increase consistent use of renewable and low-carbon fuels and substitute sources of energy in maritime transport across the Union» The scope is: «This Regulation applies to all ships of above 5 000 gross tonnage that serve the purpose of transporting passengers or cargo for commercial purposes, regardless of their flag, in respect of: (a) the energy used during their stay within a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State; (b) the entirety of the energy used on voyages from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State to a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State; (c) notwithstanding point (b), one half of the energy used on voyages arriving at or departing from a port of call located in an outermost region under the jurisdiction of a Member State; and (d) one half of the energy used on voyages arriving at or departing from a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State, where the previous or the next port of call is under the jurisdiction of a third country.»

The duty holder is the ship's company: «‘company’ means the shipowner or any other organisation or person such as the manager or the bareboat charterer, which has assumed the responsibility for the operation of the ship from the shipowner and has agreed to take over all the duties and responsibilities imposed by the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention;»

For a freight forwarder that buys ocean carriage on lanes that touch EU ports, *Analytical inference:* the duties rest on the company of each ship, because the scope and the duty-holder definition quoted above name the ship and its company; the text names no duty on a party that buys carriage. The ocean carriers whose ships serve such lanes are therefore the parties in scope, and the workspace meets the Regulation through its carrier relationships. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that charters tonnage or otherwise acts as the operator of a ship is a company under Article 3(13). Effect by cargo vertical (live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive, humanitarian) requires carrier-specific data and is not stated by the sources.

Competitive lens: the sources name no operator and state no carrier's position on compliance, so no comparison between carriers is stated. Client-conversation lens: from the quoted text the workspace can say that the duty rests on the ship's company and that the Regulation leaves the allocation of penalty cost to contract; it can ask a carrier which entity is the company and what its charging terms say, as set out in section 3.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

COST ALERT: a carrier-relations lead asks each ocean carrier on EU-touching lanes, in writing and now, to name the entity that is the company of each vessel on the lane and to confirm the plan to deliver the ship-specific report to the verifier. *Analytical inference:* the next such date is 31 January in 2027, because the verification period is the calendar year after the reporting period. The text fixes the report date: «By 31 January of the verification period, companies shall provide to the verifier a ship-specific report (the ‘FuelEU report’) containing all the information referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article and the monitoring data and documentation referred to in Article 7(4) for the reporting period.» The report covers the reporting period: «‘reporting period’ means a period from 1 January to 31 December of the year during which information referred to in this Regulation is monitored and recorded, where data for voyages starting and ending in two different calendar years is accounted under the calendar year concerned;»

*Operational implication:* the request lets the workspace see, for each lane, which party carries the penalty exposure and the document-of-compliance obligation before the reporting period closes. The sources state no consequence for cargo of a carrier missing the report date. In a client conversation the workspace can say that the duty rests on the ship's company, and can ask the carrier the questions in this section.

COST ALERT: a commercial lead asks each ocean carrier on EU-touching lanes for its FuelEU charging terms before the next rate renewal. The Regulation leaves the allocation of penalty cost to contract: «The company shall remain responsible for the payment of the FuelEU penalties, without prejudice to the possibility for the company to conclude contractual agreements with the commercial operators of the ship that provide for the liability of the commercial operators to reimburse the company for the payment of the FuelEU penalties, when the responsibility for the purchase of the fuel or the operation of the ship is assumed by the commercial operator. For the purposes of this paragraph, operation of the ship shall mean determining the cargo carried, the route and the speed of the ship.» The penalty rate in Annex IV, Part B is the figure «2 400» and its unit is stated as: «Is the amount to be paid in EUR per equivalent metric ton of VLSFO» The sources state no surcharge rate, no pass-through to cargo and no date for such a charge, so the cost to the workspace's shipments is not stated. *Analytical inference:* because Article 23(8) leaves reimbursement to contract between the company and the commercial operators of the ship, the carrier's contract wording is the place where any cargo-side charge would be set; the sources do not state that any such charge exists.

MONITORING: a carrier-relations lead asks container carriers on lanes to ports covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 whether their vessels will connect to on-shore power supply from the date in Article 6(1): «From 1 January 2030, a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call which is covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 and which is under the jurisdiction of a Member State shall connect to OPS and use it for all its electrical power demand at berth.» This is a forward-looking enquiry without a deadline for the workspace.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any of these enquiries is a contractual or regulatory duty of the workspace is a question for counsel; the text names no duty on a freight forwarder.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The roles the text defines are the company, the verifier, the administering State, the competent authorities of the Member States and the managing body of the port. The verifier is defined as «‘verifier’ means a legal entity carrying out verification activities, which is accredited by a national accreditation body pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 and this Regulation;» The administering State is defined as «‘administering State’ means a Member State determined by applying Article 3gf(1) of Directive 2003/87/EC in relation to a company within the meaning of this Regulation, without prejudice to the choice of the competent authorities in charge within the relevant Member State;»

The company may allocate penalty cost by contract with two other parties: the commercial operators of the ship (quoted in section 3) and fuel suppliers: «The company shall remain responsible for the payment of the FuelEU penalties, without prejudice to the possibility for the company to conclude contractual agreements with fuel suppliers that provide for the liability of the fuel suppliers to reimburse the company for the payment of the FuelEU penalties.»

A freight forwarder is not named. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the text defines the commercial operator by what it does, determining the cargo carried, the route and the speed of the ship; whether a forwarder that books space on a carrier's ship falls in that group is not stated and is a question for counsel. Until counsel confirms, the workspace's placement is as a buyer of carriage from companies that carry the duties.

## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

The guidance below comes from the Commission's services and is not binding: «However, the Q&A does not commit the European Commission. Moreover, it can in no way alter the legal effects of FuelEU Maritime and is without prejudice to the prerogatives of the European Court of Justice»

**Who is the company.** «The entity responsible for ensuring compliance with FuelEU Maritime Regulation should be the entity that is responsible for compliance of the ship with the International Safety Management Code (ISM Company).» *Analytical inference:* the guidance ties the duty to the party that carries the ship's safety-management responsibility, which keeps the duty with the ship's operating company and away from a party that only buys carriage. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the guidance does not address a forwarder that acts as a ship operator.

**Which ships carry the berth duty.** «These requirements will apply only to ships carrying exclusively containers, as defined in Article 3(31) and passenger ships, as defined in Article 3(29) of the Regulation.» *Analytical inference:* general cargo ships that carry containers among other cargo are outside the berth duty on this reading, so the workspace's container lanes are affected only where the vessel is a dedicated containership.

**Neighbouring ports.** «Therefore, the energy used by containerships during a stop in such ports needs to be reported as energy used at sea.»

**Norway and Iceland.** «Norwegian and Icelandic ports will be regarded as third-country ports in a FuelEU context from 1 January 2025 until the incorporation of FuelEU in the EEA Agreement.» *Analytical inference:* a voyage between an EU port and a Norwegian or Icelandic port falls in the third-country case of Article 2(1), point (d), until incorporation; the hub gives no date for incorporation.

**Penalty collection.** «The administering state of the company ensures the payment of the penalty, without prejudice to possible contractual agreements between companies and commercial operators or fuel suppliers to handle the liability.» The quoted answer gives no information on how a company charges the cost onward.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

**Implementing act on OPS communication.** Issuing body: the Commission. «The following implementing acts are upcoming, and public feedback will be requested soon: Implementing act on OPS communication» Expected date: none is sourced. It will address the information a ship gives before it connects to OPS under Article 6(8). Sections 8 and 10 will need updating when it is adopted. The workspace has nothing to decide until the content is published. *Analytical inference:* the act sets the form of the pre-arrival notice, so carrier port-call procedures for container lanes depend on it.

**Implementing act on zero-emission technology criteria.** Issuing body: the Commission. «Implementing act on the criteria for the acceptance of zero-emission technologies» The Regulation set an earlier date: «For the list of existing technologies provided for in Annex III, those implementing acts shall be adopted by 30 June 2024, where applicable.» Expected date: none is sourced. *Analytical inference:* the hub still lists the act as upcoming, which shows that the act has not been adopted although Article 6(7) set 30 June 2024 for the existing list where applicable.

**Evaluation report.** Issuing body: the Commission. «By 31 December 2027, and every five years thereafter at the latest, the Commission shall report to the European Parliament and the Council the results of an evaluation as regards the functioning of this Regulation, including possible impacts of market distortions or port evasion; as regards the evolution of the zero-emission technologies in maritime transport and their market, as well as the evolution of the technologies and market for renewable and low-carbon fuels and for OPS, including at anchorage; as regards the use of revenue generated by the FuelEU penalties; and as regards the impact of this Regulation on the competitiveness of the maritime sector in the Union.» The evaluation may be accompanied by a proposal to amend the Regulation. The text does not say whether any of the limits in section 8 will change; what the sources do not state is left open.

**Renewable fuels of non-biological origin subtarget.** Issuing body: the Commission, from monitoring data. «If the share of RFNBO referred to in paragraph 2 is less than 1 % for the reporting period 2031, a subtarget of 2 % shall apply for such fuels in the yearly energy used on board by a ship from 1 January 2034, subject to paragraph 5.» The text makes the subtarget conditional on that monitoring result.

**Global measure from the IMO.** Issuing body: the Commission, if the IMO acts. «In the event of the adoption by the IMO of a global GHG fuel standard or global GHG intensity limits for the energy used on board by ships, the Commission shall, without delay, present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council.» No adoption date is sourced.

**Report on interaction with Regulation (EU) 2015/757.** «By 23 September 2024, the Commission shall present a report to the European Parliament and to the Council examining the interaction and convergence between this Regulation and Regulation (EU) 2015/757 or any other sectoral legal acts.» The captured sources do not state whether this report was presented.

*Analytical inference:* none of these events changes a workspace obligation, because the text names none; each can change the cost or procedure borne by carriers.

## 7. Threshold Questions

**Does a stop count as a port of call?** A stop that is not a port of call changes whose energy counts and where. The test for a neighbouring container transhipment port is: «The implementing acts referred to in the first subparagraph shall list a port as a neighbouring container transhipment port where the share of transhipment of containers, measured in 20 foot equivalent units, exceeds 65 % of the total container traffic of that port during the most recent 12-month period for which relevant data are available and where that port is located outside the Union but less than 300 nautical miles from a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State.» The consequence is in the definition: «and stops of containerships in a neighbouring container transhipment port listed in the implementing act adopted pursuant to Article 2(2);» The hub confirms the list exists: «The implementing regulation on neighbouring container transhipment ports in relation to the FuelEU has been published. Stops made in the ports included on the list will not be counted as “port of call” under the FuelEU maritime regulation.» *Legal Confirmation Required:* which ports are on the list is not stated in the captured sources; counsel or the implementing regulation itself must be checked for any transhipment hub on the workspace's lanes. *Analytical inference:* a container lane routed through a listed port treats that stop as part of the voyage, as the guidance quoted in section 5 says.

**Is the vessel a containership for the berth duty?** The definition is: «‘containership’ means a ship designed exclusively for the carriage of containers in holds and on deck;» The guidance quoted in section 5 reads this to exclude general cargo ships that carry containers. What is decided: the definition and the guidance reading. What requires confirmation: the status of a vessel type that carries containers and other cargo; *Legal Confirmation Required:* the question for counsel is whether a given mixed-cargo vessel is a containership under Article 3(31).

**Who is the company?** The definition and the guidance are quoted in sections 2 and 5. The text and the guidance leave open the status of a forwarder that acts as the operator of a ship; *Legal Confirmation Required:* the question for counsel is whether a forwarder is a company or a commercial operator under Articles 3(13) and 23(8).

## 8. Substantive Requirements

**GHG intensity limit (Article 4).** Cause: the Regulation sets a yearly cap on the GHG intensity of the energy a ship uses. «The yearly average GHG intensity of the energy used on board by a ship during a reporting period shall not exceed the limit set out in paragraph 2.» The reference value is named in the guidance as «reference value of 91,16 grams of CO2 equivalent per MJ». The limit is that value, reduced by the following percentages: «— 2 % from 1 January 2025; — 6 % from 1 January 2030; — 14,5 % from 1 January 2035; — 31 % from 1 January 2040; — 62 % from 1 January 2045; — 80 % from 1 January 2050.» Mechanical consequence: the Regulation defines the deficit as follows: «‘compliance deficit’ means a compliance balance with a negative value;» A company with a deficit on 1 June of the verification period pays the penalty described below, after any banking, borrowing or pooling. Effect by vertical: the sources state no effect on live events, artwork, luxury goods, film and television, automotive or humanitarian cargo; the effect requires carrier-specific data. *Analytical inference:* the step from 2025 to 2030 is the next scheduled tightening, as the quoted text shows.

**Renewable fuels of non-biological origin (Article 5).** «from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2033 a multiplier of ‘2’ can be used to reward the ship for the use of RFNBO» The article carries a conditional subtarget: «If the share of RFNBO referred to in paragraph 2 is less than 1 % for the reporting period 2031, a subtarget of 2 % shall apply for such fuels in the yearly energy used on board by a ship from 1 January 2034, subject to paragraph 5.» The article also states: «This Article shall not apply to the share of yearly energy used on board by ships from OPS.» The multiplier is a calculation rule for the ship's intensity; the sources state no cargo cost from it.

**Berth duty (Article 6).** «Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall apply to: (a) containerships; (b) passenger ships.» The dated steps are from 1 January 2030 at ports covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804, quoted in section 3, and from 1 January 2035 at other ports: «From 1 January 2035, a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call which is not covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804, which is under the jurisdiction of a Member State and where the quay is equipped with available OPS shall connect to that OPS and use it for all its electrical power demand at berth.» Member States may also apply the duty earlier: «From 1 January 2030 and until 31 December 2034, and after consulting relevant stakeholders, including, where appropriate, the managing body of the port, a Member State may decide that a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call under its jurisdiction which is not covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804, or in certain parts of such port, shall connect to OPS and use it for all its electrical power demand at berth.» The sources state no cost to cargo from the berth duty.

**Penalties (Article 23 and Annex IV).** Cause: a GHG intensity deficit or a non-compliant port call. Mechanical consequence for the company: «the company shall pay by 30 June of the verification period an amount equal to the FuelEU penalty resulting from the application of the formulas specified in Part B of Annex IV.» For a non-compliant port call: «an amount equal to the FuelEU penalty resulting from the multiplication of EUR 1,5 by the established total electrical power demand of the ship at berth and by the total number of hours rounded up to the nearest whole hour, spent at berth by the ship in non-compliance with the requirements set out in Article 6.» The amount in Annex IV, Part B, is quoted in section 3. Effect on cargo: the sources do not state how or whether the penalty reaches an invoice; the company may seek reimbursement by contract, as quoted in sections 3 and 4.

**Document of compliance and enforcement (Articles 22, 24 and 25).** «By 30 June of the verification period, ships calling at a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State, arriving at, staying within or departing from a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State, or which have carried out voyages during the corresponding reporting period, shall hold a valid FuelEU document of compliance.» Enforcement follows a ladder: «Where a ship fails to comply with the obligation set out in Article 24 for two or more consecutive reporting periods, and where other enforcement measures have failed to ensure compliance with this Regulation, the competent authority of the Member State of the port of call may, in respect of a ship not flying the flag of that Member State and after giving the opportunity to the company concerned to submit its observations, issue an expulsion order.» Mechanical consequence for cargo: the sources state none; the expulsion order bears on the ship, and its effect on a shipment is not stated.

**Flexibility (Articles 20 and 21).** Banking: «the company may bank it to the same ship’s compliance balance for the following reporting period.» Pooling: «of two or more ships, as calculated in accordance with Article 16(4), may be pooled for the purposes of complying with the requirements set out in Article 4» Borrowing: «the company may borrow an advance compliance surplus of the corresponding amount from the following reporting period. The advance compliance surplus shall be added to the ship’s compliance balance in the reporting period and the advance compliance surplus multiplied by 1,1 shall be subtracted from the same ship’s compliance balance in the following reporting period.»

**Scope exclusions (Article 2).** «This Regulation does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries, fish-catching or fish-processing ships, wooden ships of a primitive build, ships not propelled by mechanical means, or ships owned or operated by a government and used only for non-commercial purposes.»

**Application dates (Article 32).** «It shall apply from 1 January 2025, with the exception of Articles 8 and 9 which shall apply from 31 August 2024.»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the GHG intensity limit, the berth duty and the penalties bind the company of each ship; whether a freight forwarder that determines the cargo carried, the route and the speed of a ship is a commercial operator under Article 23(8), and whether any duty or liability then reaches it, is a question for counsel. Whether a given vessel is a containership for Article 6 is also a question for counsel.

No phase-in is stated beyond the dated steps above. Obligations surveyed: 19; workspace-adjacent: 4; extracted as FACT: 19.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The reporting duties sit with the company of each ship, the verifiers and the competent authorities, not with a freight forwarder. *Analytical inference:* the workspace has no registration to make under the text quoted here.

**Monitoring plan.** «By 31 August 2024, companies shall submit to the verifiers a monitoring plan for each of their ships» «For ships falling under the scope of this Regulation for the first time after 31 August 2024, companies shall submit a monitoring plan to the verifier without undue delay and no later than two months after each ship’s first call at a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State.»

**Monitoring and recording.** «As of 1 January 2025, based on the monitoring plan referred to in Article 8 and following the assessment of that plan by the verifier, companies shall monitor and record, for each ship arriving at or departing from a port of call, and for each voyage referred to in Article 2(1), the following information:» The listed data begin: «(a) port of departure and port of arrival including the date and time of departure and arrival and time spent at berth; (b) for each ship to which Article 6(1) applies, the connection to and use of OPS or the application of any of the exceptions provided for in Article 6(5) as confirmed pursuant to Article 6(9), point (a), where applicable; (c) the amount of each type of fuel consumed at berth and at sea; (d) the amount of electricity delivered to the ship through OPS;»

**Annual report.** The ship-specific FuelEU report date is quoted in section 3.

**Pool registration.** «By 30 April of the verification period, the selected verifier shall record in the FuelEU database the definitive composition of the pool»

**Database.** «The Commission shall develop, ensure the functioning of and update an electronic database for the monitoring of compliance with this Regulation» Its use is stated as: «shall be used to keep a record of actions related to verification activities, of the compliance balance of ships, including use of the flexibility mechanisms set out in Articles 20 and 21, of the application of the exceptions set out in Article 6(5), of actions related to payment of the FuelEU penalties imposed under Article 23 and of the issuance of the FuelEU document of compliance.»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* the text does not say whether a forwarder with its own chartered tonnage has a registration or reporting duty; counsel should confirm for any such case.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the Regulation requires companies to build record-keeping and notification routines; the gap for a forwarder is a data field, not a system build.

**What the Regulation requires of a company.** «Companies shall obtain, analyse and store, for at least five years, all monitoring data and documentation» «Ships shall inform in advance the competent authority of the Member State of the port of call or any duly authorised entity prior to entry into ports about their intention to connect to OPS or their intention to use a zero-emission technology in application of paragraph 5, point (b). Ships that intend to connect to OPS shall also indicate the amount of power they expect to require during that port call.» For a carrier with manual or voyage-level records and no per-ship data store, *Analytical inference:* the gap to these requirements is operational and sits with the carrier.

**What the workspace adds.**

- At the next carrier onboarding round, a procurement lead adds to the ocean carrier onboarding and rate-request form a field for the name of the FuelEU company of each vessel on the lane and the date of its current document of compliance.
- At the next sustainability-report cycle, a sustainability-reporting lead asks carriers whether ship-level GHG intensity data under the Regulation can be supplied for the workspace's emissions reporting. The FuelEU database is described as follows: «It shall be accessible to the companies, the verifiers, the competent authorities and any duly authorised entity, the national accreditation bodies, the European Maritime Safety Agency established by Regulation (EC) No 1406/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 24 ) and the Commission, with appropriate access rights» A forwarder is not among the parties listed, so the carrier is the route to the data.

*Operational implication:* these steps use only dates and roles the text states and no cost figure.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

**Island routes.** «Member States may exempt from the application of paragraph 1, points (a) and (b) specific routes and ports in respect of the energy used on voyages performed by passenger ships other than cruise passenger ships between a port of call under the jurisdiction of a Member State and a port of call under the jurisdiction of the same Member State located on an island with fewer than 200 000 permanent residents, and in respect of the energy used during their stay within a port of call of that island. No such exemptions shall apply beyond 31 December 2029. Prior to the entry into force of those exemptions, Member States shall notify them to the Commission. The Commission shall publish those exemptions in the Official Journal of the European Union» Outermost regions: «Member States may exempt from the application of paragraph 1, points (a) and (c) specific routes and ports in respect of the energy used by ships on voyages between a port of call located in an outermost region and another port of call located in an outermost region» The quoted text for island routes includes the notification before the exemption takes effect and the publication by the Commission in the Official Journal. *Analytical inference:* an exemption helps the workspace only if its shipments move on an exempt passenger-ship route.

**Berth exceptions.** «Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall not apply to ships that: (a) are moored at the quayside for less than two hours, calculated on the basis of time of arrival and time of departure monitored and recorded in accordance with Article 15; (b) use zero-emission technologies» The full list is in Article 6(5). A cap applies from 2035: «From 1 January 2035, in ports falling under the requirements of Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804, it shall only be possible to apply the exceptions provided for in paragraph 5, points (d), (e) and (f) to a maximum number of port calls corresponding to 10 % of a ship’s total number of port calls that took place during a reporting period, rounded up to the nearest whole number, where relevant, or to a maximum of 10 port calls during the relevant reporting period, whichever is lower.»

**Ice conditions.** «the company may request, until 31 December 2034, to exclude the additional energy consumption, due to sailing in ice conditions.»

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a given route or vessel falls in an exemption is a question for counsel and for the Member State notice published in the Official Journal.

## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

*Industry interpretation:* the row for 31 January 2026 quotes a classification society's page, which applies the Regulation's recurring annual dates to the first reporting period; the Regulation itself states the recurring dates in Articles 15, 16, 20, 21, 22 and 23 without a year.

- 13 September 2023: the Regulation is adopted at Strasbourg, as quoted in section 1
- 22 September 2023: the Regulation is published in the Official Journal at OJ L 234, as quoted in section 1
- 12 October 2023: the Regulation enters into force on the twentieth day after publication («shall be conferred on the Commission for an indeterminate period of time from 12 October 2023»)
- 30 June 2024: the date set for implementing acts on the list of existing zero-emission technologies, where applicable («those implementing acts shall be adopted by 30 June 2024, where applicable.»)
- 26 July 2024: the Commission adopts the verification activities act and the monitoring plan template act («Commission implementing regulation (EU) 2024/2027of 26 July 2024»; «Commission implementing regulation (EU) 2024/2031 of 26 July 2024»)
- 31 August 2024: Articles 8 and 9 on the monitoring plan begin to apply and monitoring plans are due, as quoted in section 10
- 9 September 2024: the Commission adopts the verifier accreditation act («Commission delegated regulation (EU) 2025/192 of 9 September 2024»)
- 23 September 2024: date set for the Commission report on interaction with Regulation (EU) 2015/757, quoted in section 6
- 1 January 2025: the Regulation applies in full; the first limit, 2 % below the reference value, and monitoring and recording begin, as quoted in section 8
- 6 June 2025: the Commission adopts the act on neighbouring container transhipment ports («Commission implementing regulation (EU) 2025/1127 of 6 June 2025»)
- 31 December 2025: the date set for the Commission to adopt the list of neighbouring container transhipment ports («By 31 December 2025, the Commission shall adopt implementing acts establishing a list of neighbouring container transhipment ports.»)
- 31 January 2026: «Submit the individual ship’s FuelEU reports by 31 January 2026. By 30 April 2026, have the compliance balance approved in the FuelEU Maritime database. By 30 June 2026, have the FuelEU Document of Compliance on board. This is also the penalty payment deadline.»
- 23 February 2026: the Commission adopts the act on FuelEU database access rights («Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/394 of 23 February 2026»)
- 30 April 2026: the classification society's page gives this date for approval of the compliance balance in the FuelEU database, in the row above
- 30 June 2026: the classification society's page gives this date for holding the document of compliance and for penalty payment, in the row above
- 31 December 2027: Commission evaluation report on the functioning of the Regulation, quoted in section 6
- 31 December 2029: exemptions under Article 2 expire at the latest, quoted in section 12
- 1 January 2030: the limit falls to 6 % below the reference value and the berth duty starts at ports covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804, as quoted in sections 3 and 8
- 31 December 2033: the multiplier of 2 for RFNBO ends, as quoted in section 8
- 1 January 2034: the conditional RFNBO subtarget of 2 % applies if triggered, as quoted in section 6
- 31 December 2034: the ice-conditions exclusion ends, as quoted in section 12
- 1 January 2035: the limit falls to 14,5 % below the reference value and the berth duty extends to other ports with available OPS, as quoted in section 8
- 1 January 2040: the limit falls to 31 % below the reference value, as quoted in section 8
- 1 January 2045: the limit falls to 62 % below the reference value, as quoted in section 8
- 1 January 2050: the limit falls to 80 % below the reference value, as quoted in section 8

Entry into force rule: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union»
